content: UN numbers, also referred to as UN IDs, are four-digit numerical codes used to identify hazardous substances and articles, such as explosives, flammable liquids, and toxic substances, within the context of international transportation. Certain hazardous substances are assigned unique UN numbers; for example, acrylamide is designated as UN2074. In other cases, groups of chemicals or products with similar hazardous properties are assigned a shared UN number. For instance, flammable liquids that are not otherwise specified are categorized under UN1993. If a chemical exists in both solid and liquid states, it may be assigned different UN numbers for each state, provided their hazardous properties differ significantly. Similarly, substances with varying levels of purity or differing concentrations in solution may also receive distinct UN numbers. The range of UN numbers spans from UN0001 to approximately UN3500. These numbers are allocated by the United Nations Committee of Experts on the Transport of Dangerous Goods and are documented in their Recommendations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods, commonly referred to as the Orange Book. These recommendations are subsequently adopted by regulatory organizations responsible for overseeing various modes of transportation. For further reference, a comprehensive list of UN numbers is available. In North America, a similar system exists, where NA numbers (also known as DOT numbers) are issued by the United States Department of Transportation. NA numbers are generally identical to UN numbers, with the exception that certain substances lacking a UN number may be assigned an NA number. These additional NA numbers fall within the range of NA8000 to NA9999. Each UN number is associated with a hazard identifier, which specifies the general hazard class and its subdivision. In the case of explosives, the hazard identifier also includes the compatibility group. For example, the hazard identifier for acrylamide is 6.1, while that for cigarette lighters is 2.1. If a substance presents multiple hazards, additional subsidiary risk identifiers may be provided. It is important to note that the hazard class or classes of a substance cannot be inferred directly from its UN number; instead, this information must be obtained from a corresponding reference table.
